source_text: I. Quotiescumque servorum dei gloriosa facta memoramus, illi referimus gratiam qui et patientem tuetur in poena et victorem coronat in gloria. Martianus itaque consularis a Decio imperatore praefectus, Christianae legis inimicus, Achatium ad se iussit adduci, quem [secutum — sense: a follower and support; R reads Antiochiae regionis for illius religionis] quoddam ac refugium illius religionis audierat, et eo introducto ad se ait: Debes amare principes nostros, homo Romanis legibus vivens. respondit Achatius: Et cui magis cordi est vel a quo sic diligitur imperator, quemadmodum ab hominibus Christianis? assidua enim nobis est pro eo ac iugis oratio, ut prolixum aevum in hac luce conficiat ac iusta populos potestate moderetur et pacatum maxime imperii sui tempus accipiat; deinde pro salute militum et pro statu mundi et orbis. Martianus ait: Haec et ipse collaudo; sed ut obsequium tuum plenius imperator agnoscat, sacrificium illi solve nobiscum. Achatius dixit: Ego dominum meum, qui est verus et magnus, pro salute regis obtestor, sacrificium vero nec ille exigere, nec nos debemus exsolvere. quis enim homini sacra persoluat?
thought_title: Christians pray for the emperor but sacrifice only to God
orientation: Martianus the prefect interrogates Achatius, who argues Christians honor the emperor by constant prayer for his life and rule.
pass_a_gloss: Whenever we recall the glorious deeds of the servants of God, we give thanks to him who both protects the suffering one in punishment and crowns the victor in glory. Martianus therefore, consular prefect under Decius the emperor, enemy of the Christian faith, ordered Achatius to be brought to him, whom he had heard was a certain follower and refuge of that religion, and when he had been led in to him he said: You ought to love our rulers, man living under Roman laws. Achatius answered: And to whom is he more at heart or by whom is the emperor so loved as by Christian men? For constant and continual prayer is ours for him, that he may complete a long life in this light and may rule peoples with just power and may receive a most peaceful time of his empire; then for the safety of the soldiers and for the condition of the world and the earth. Martianus said: These things I myself also praise; but so that the emperor may recognize your obedience more fully, pay sacrifice to him with us. Achatius said: I beseech my lord, who is true and great, for the safety of the king, but as for sacrifice neither ought he to demand it nor ought we to pay it. For who would pay sacred rites to a man?

pass_b_english: Whenever we recall the glorious deeds of God's servants, we give thanks to Him who guards the sufferer in his punishment and crowns the victor in his glory.

Martianus, a prefect of consular rank appointed by the Emperor Decius and an enemy of the Christian faith, ordered Achatius to be brought before him, for he had heard that Achatius was a follower and a refuge of that faith. When Achatius was led in, Martianus said to him, "As a man who lives under Roman laws, you ought to love our rulers."

Achatius answered, "Who holds the emperor more dear, and by whom is he so loved, as he is by Christians? Our prayer for him is constant and unceasing, that he may live a long life in this world, that he may govern the peoples with just power and enjoy a time of peace above all in his reign, and then that the soldiers may be kept safe and the world and the earth may stand secure."

Martianus said, "This I praise as well, but so that the emperor may know your loyalty more fully, pay sacrifice to him along with us." Achatius said, "I beseech my Lord, who is true and great, for the safety of the king, but sacrifice neither does He demand nor ought we to pay in full. For who would pay sacred rites to a man?"
notes: The phrase quem [secutum] quoddam ac refugium illius religionis is damaged and uncertain; gloss follows the supplied sense of a follower and support, with R variant Antiochiae regionis for illius religionis noted but not translated as source.

last_rejected.quote: sacrifice neither does He demand nor ought we to pay in full
last_rejected.source_quote: sacrificium vero nec ille exigere, nec nos debemus exsolvere
last_rejected.why: "ille" most naturally means the king/emperor, as the next question about sacred rites to a man shows. Capital "He" makes God the one who does not demand sacrifice.
last_rejected.fix: but sacrifice he does not demand, nor ought we to pay it. For who would pay sacred rites to a man?
last_rejected.ruling: ille can refer to dominum meum; homini clause fits either reading, so He is defensible
